key_terms.meaning: Input where V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub>; V<sub>M</sub> = (V<sub>DD</sub> + rV<sub>tn</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|)/(1 + r), r = √(k<sub>n</sub>/k<sub>p</sub>).

NM<sub>H</sub> = V<sub>OH</sub> − V<sub>IH</sub>, NM<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>IL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>; V<sub>IL</sub>, V<sub>IH</sub> where the slope is −1. Matched: V<sub>IL</sub> = (3V<sub>DD</sub> + 2V<sub>t</sub>)/8.
nMOS load with gate at V<sub>DD</sub>; V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>t</sub> (lower with body effect); ratioed.
Always-on loads giving V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>; V<sub>OL</sub> > 0 set by the strength ratio; static current when the output is low.
Output moving between 10% and 90% of V<sub>DD</sub>; 2.2RC for a single RC.
d = gh + p; path effort F = GBH; best stage effort F<sup>1/N</sup>; D = NF<sup>1/N</sup> + P.
R<sub>□</sub> = ρ/t in Ω/□; wire R = R<sub>□</sub> × L/W.
Plate + fringe + coupling, about 0.2 fF/µm; coupling counts double when the neighbour switches the opposite way.
50% delay 0.38RC (lumped 0.69RC); grows as L², so long wires get repeaters.
τ<sub>Di</sub> = Σ C<sub>k</sub>R<sub>ik</sub> (shared path resistance); delay ≈ 0.69τ<sub>D</sub>; RC/2 for a uniform wire.
P = αC V<sub>DD</sub>²f, α = probability of a 0 → 1 transition per cycle.
Lower V and f together; power scales as (V<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>1</sub>)²(f<sub>2</sub>/f<sub>1</sub>), energy per operation as (V<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>1</sub>)².
Header or footer switch cuts leakage of an idle block; worth it only beyond the break-even time = wake energy ÷ leakage power.
Dual pull-up and pull-down networks; 2N transistors, full swing, no static current.
nMOS (C) ∥ pMOS (C̄); passes both rails; nMOS alone passes a 1 only to V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>.
V<sub>X</sub> = (C<sub>X</sub>V<sub>DD</sub> + C<sub>int</sub>V<sub>int</sub>)/(C<sub>X</sub> + C<sub>int</sub>) on a dynamic node.
Dynamic gate plus static inverter; non-inverting, outputs only rise during evaluation, so stages can be chained.

takeaways: The VTC gives V<sub>M</sub>, V<sub>IL</sub>, V<sub>IH</sub> and both noise margins; a matched inverter (k<sub>n</sub> = k<sub>p</sub>) has V<sub>M</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>/2, which needs a pMOS about µ<sub>n</sub>/µ<sub>p</sub> times wider.
NMOS inverters need a load; every load draws static current when the output is low, and only the enhancement load loses a threshold at the top.

Delay is charge over current: t<sub>PHL</sub> ≈ C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>/(2I<sub>Dsat</sub>), and the RC model with R<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 0.75V<sub>DD</sub>/I<sub>Dsat</sub> agrees within a few per cent.
Logical effort sizes a path for least delay: equal stage effort F<sup>1/N</sup>, about 4 per stage.
Wire resistance is R<sub>□</sub>L/W, wire capacitance about 0.2 fF/µm, and a distributed wire's own delay is 0.38RC, growing as length squared.
The Elmore delay Σ C<sub>k</sub>R<sub>ik</sub> handles RC trees and transistor stacks by hand; put the latest input nearest the output.
Power is αCV<sub>DD</sub>²f plus short-circuit plus V<sub>DD</sub>I<sub>leak</sub>; leakage wins below the crossover frequency.
Low-power design attacks each term: lower V<sub>DD</sub> (DVFS, parallelism), lower α (clock gating), lower leakage (power gating beyond break-even, high-V<sub>t</sub> cells).
Static CMOS is robust and default; ratioed, pass-transistor and dynamic styles save transistors or time but pay with static current, weak levels, or clocking and charge sharing.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the inverter transfer curve with noise margins, a delay or power calculation, the Elmore delay of a network, and a comparison of logic styles (static, ratioed, pass-transistor, dynamic and domino) with transistor-level circuits.

bank.q: Draw the voltage transfer characteristic of a CMOS inverter and explain its five regions. Derive the switching threshold V<sub>M</sub> and find V<sub>M</sub>, V<sub>IL</sub>, V<sub>IH</sub> and the noise margins for a matched inverter with V<sub>DD</sub> = 2.5 V and V<sub>tn</sub> = |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.5 V.
outline: VTC axes and the five regions with transistor states
equal currents at V<sub>M</sub>, both saturated, the V<sub>M</sub> formula
answer: Circuit: the pMOS source at V<sub>DD</sub>, the nMOS source at ground, gates joined as the input, drains joined as the output. In steady state the two drain currents are equal, which fixes V<sub>out</sub> for each V<sub>in</sub>.

answer.text: Five regions (sketch the curve: flat at V<sub>DD</sub>, steep fall through V<sub>M</sub>, flat at 0 V):
Derivation of V<sub>M</sub>: both devices saturated, so
answer.pre:
(k<sub>n</sub>/2)(V<sub>M</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>)² = (k<sub>p</sub>/2)(V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>M</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|)²
r(V<sub>M</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>) = V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>M</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|,   r = √(k<sub>n</sub>/k<sub>p</sub>)
V<sub>M</sub> = (V<sub>DD</sub> + rV<sub>tn</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|)/(1 + r)

answer: Definitions: V<sub>OH</sub> and V<sub>OL</sub> are the flat output levels (V<sub>DD</sub> and 0 V). V<sub>IL</sub> and V<sub>IH</sub> are the inputs where dV<sub>out</sub>/dV<sub>in</sub> = −1. NM<sub>H</sub> = V<sub>OH</sub> − V<sub>IH</sub>, NM<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>IL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>.
For the matched case (r = 1, V<sub>t</sub> = 0.5 V): V<sub>M</sub> = (2.5 + 0.5 − 0.5)/2 = 1.25 V.

answer.text: Slope −1 points for a matched inverter:

answer: Noise margins: NM<sub>L</sub> = 1.0625 − 0 = 1.06 V and NM<sub>H</sub> = 2.5 − 1.4375 = 1.06 V, equal because the inverter is symmetric.

Effect of sizing: with equal widths k<sub>n</sub> ≈ 2.5k<sub>p</sub>, r = 1.58 and V<sub>M</sub> = (2.5 + 0.79 − 0.5)/2.58 = 1.08 V; the curve moves left, NM<sub>L</sub> falls and NM<sub>H</sub> rises. A pMOS 2.5 times wider restores V<sub>M</sub> = 1.25 V.
Check: V<sub>IL</sub> < V<sub>M</sub> < V<sub>IH</sub> (1.06 < 1.25 < 1.44 V) and the two margins add to V<sub>DD</sub> − (V<sub>IH</sub> − V<sub>IL</sub>) = 2.5 − 0.375 = 2.125 V = 2 × 1.0625 V.

Regions at V<sub>M</sub>: with V<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>out</sub> = 1.25 V the nMOS has V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.25 V > V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.75 V and the pMOS has V<sub>SD</sub> = 1.25 V > 0.75 V, so both are saturated, as region C requires.

Output at the slope points: solving region B at V<sub>in</sub> = 1.0625 V gives V<sub>out</sub> = 2.31 V, and by symmetry V<sub>out</sub> = 0.19 V at V<sub>IH</sub>. Between these inputs the gain is above 1, so a noisy input comes out closer to a rail; this regeneration keeps levels clean along a chain of gates.

bank.q: With circuit diagrams, compare the resistive, enhancement, depletion and pseudo-nMOS loads of an NMOS inverter on V<sub>OH</sub>, V<sub>OL</sub>, static current, speed and process cost. Why did CMOS replace them?
outline: circuit of each load over one nMOS driver
V<sub>OH</sub> of each (threshold loss for the enhancement load, body effect)
V<sub>OL</sub> set by a ratio, driver linear
speed of pull-up and process steps
CMOS: no static current, full swing
answer: Common structure: an nMOS driver from output to ground with the input on its gate, and a load from V<sub>DD</sub> to the output (sketch the four circuits of Figure 3.2.1).

Resistor: V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>. V<sub>OL</sub> from (V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>)/R<sub>L</sub> = k<sub>n</sub>[(V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>)V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2]; with 5 V, 100 kΩ, 20 µA/V², 0.8 V this gives 0.57 V and 44 µA. Needs a very large resistor, so it is area-hungry.

Enhancement load (gate at V<sub>DD</sub>): always saturated; it cuts off at V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>t</sub>, so V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>t</sub> = 4.2 V, lower again with body effect because its source is the output. With k<sub>D</sub>/k<sub>L</sub> = 9, V<sub>OL</sub> = 0.22 V and 159 µA flows. Slow pull-up near the top because the load turns off. With body effect (V<sub>t0</sub> = 0.8 V, γ = 0.4 V<sup>1/2</sup>, 2φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.6 V), solving V<sub>OH</sub> = 5 − V<sub>t</sub>(V<sub>OH</sub>) by iteration gives V<sub>t</sub> = 1.32 V and V<sub>OH</sub> = 3.68 V, a loss of more than a quarter of the supply.

Depletion load (gate tied to source, V<sub>GS</sub> = 0): negative threshold, always on, V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>; nearly constant-current pull-up I<sub>DSS</sub>, so faster rising edges. With I<sub>DSS</sub> = 20 µA and k<sub>n</sub> = 100 µA/V², V<sub>OL</sub> = 0.048 V. Needs an extra implant step.
Pseudo-nMOS (pMOS, gate at 0 V): V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>; saturated while V<sub>OL</sub> ≤ |V<sub>tp</sub>|; V<sub>OL</sub> set by k<sub>n</sub>/k<sub>p</sub>. No extra process step in CMOS.

answer.text: Summary:

answer: All four are ratioed: the driver must be several times stronger than the load to get a low V<sub>OL</sub>, so areas and input capacitances grow, and every gate with its output low burns V<sub>DD</sub> × I. At 44 µA per gate, 20,000 gates with their outputs low draw 0.88 A, about 4.4 W at 5 V.

CMOS replaced them because its pull-up turns off when the pull-down is on: V<sub>OL</sub> = 0 V, V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>, sizes are not ratioed for correctness, and the only static current is leakage. Ratioed loads survive only where a small wide gate matters more than static power (PLA and ROM NOR planes).

bank.q: Explain the resistance, capacitance and inductance of an on-chip wire and the lumped, distributed RC, π and transmission-line wire models. A wire on a layer with R<sub>□</sub> = 0.08 Ω/□ is 0.25 µm wide and 2 mm long, with 0.2 fF/µm of capacitance. Find R, C and its own delay by the lumped, distributed and Elmore models.
outline: plate, fringe, coupling capacitance; Miller factor
lumped C, lumped RC, distributed RC, π ladder, RLC line
answer: Resistance: R = ρL/(Wt). With layer thickness fixed, R<sub>□</sub> = ρ/t and R = R<sub>□</sub> × (number of squares L/W). Copper (bulk 1.7 µΩ·cm) is used because it beats aluminium; narrow lines have a higher effective resistivity.

Capacitance: plate C<sub>pp</sub> = εWL/h to the layer below; fringe from the sidewalls and edges; coupling C<sub>c</sub> to neighbours, which acts as 2C<sub>c</sub> when a neighbour switches the opposite way and as 0 when it switches the same way. Total is about 0.2 fF/µm in a dense layer.

Inductance matters only for low-resistance wires (wide clocks and power rails) with edges faster than about 2.5 times the time of flight (light in oxide moves about 1.5 × 10⁸ m/s). Thin signal wires are RC.

answer.text: Models:

head: Model
Use
Own 50% delay
rows: C/2 – R – C/2 per section, for simulation
matches the distributed line with a few sections

answer.text: Numbers:

answer: π model: 200 fF – 640 Ω – 200 fF; its Elmore delay at the far end is 640 × 200 fF = 128 ps, the same RC/2.

Comparison: the lumped model overstates the wire's own delay by 82% (176.6 against 97.3 ps); Elmore's RC/2 overstates the exact 0.38RC by about 30% but is safe and easy. Delay grows as L²: the same wire at 4 mm would have 4 × 97.3 = 389 ps of its own delay, so long wires get repeaters.

Coupling: if half of the 0.2 fF/µm is coupling to the two neighbours, it counts as 0.1 + 2 × 0.1 = 0.3 fF/µm when both switch the opposite way, giving 600 fF and 0.38 × 640 Ω × 600 fF = 146 ps, and as 0.1 fF/µm (200 fF, 48.6 ps) when both switch the same way. The same wire can therefore be three times slower depending on its neighbours, which is why timing tools analyse crosstalk.

With a driver: a 1 kΩ driver and a 20 fF gate at the far end give 0.69 × 1 kΩ × 420 fF + 0.38 × 640 Ω × 400 fF + 0.69 × 640 Ω × 20 fF = 289.8 + 97.3 + 8.8 = 395.9 ps. The wire's own term is about a quarter of this; the driver charging the wire capacitance is the largest part, so for this length a stronger driver helps more than a repeater.

bank.q: List the components of power dissipation in a CMOS circuit with a formula for each. Explain why switching energy is CV<sub>DD</sub>² per 0 → 1 transition, what the activity factor is, and which component dominates at high and low clock rates.
outline: switching power and the energy argument
answer: Total: P = αCV<sub>DD</sub>²f + P<sub>sc</sub> + V<sub>DD</sub>I<sub>leak</sub>.

Switching energy: when the output rises the supply delivers Q = CV<sub>DD</sub> at V<sub>DD</sub>, energy CV<sub>DD</sub>². The capacitor stores ½CV<sub>DD</sub>²; the other half is heat in the pMOS. On the fall, the stored half becomes heat in the nMOS. So each 0 → 1 transition costs CV<sub>DD</sub>², independent of transistor size.
Activity factor α: probability of a 0 → 1 transition per cycle. Clock α = 1; data toggling every cycle 0.5; random data 0.25. Glitches add transitions.

Short-circuit power: during an input ramp both transistors conduct while V<sub>tn</sub> < V<sub>in</sub> < V<sub>DD</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|. For a symmetric inverter P<sub>sc</sub> ≈ (k/12)(V<sub>DD</sub> − 2V<sub>t</sub>)³t<sub>r</sub>f; with k = 100 µA/V², 1.8 V, 0.5 V, 100 ps and 100 MHz it is 42.7 nW. Kept small with sharp, matched edges; zero if V<sub>DD</sub> < 2V<sub>t</sub>.

Leakage: subthreshold (rises tenfold per S ≈ 80 to 100 mV drop in V<sub>t</sub>, and with temperature), gate tunnelling through thin oxide, and reverse junction leakage. P<sub>static</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>I<sub>leak</sub>; ratioed gates add their load current.

answer.text: Example with numbers (C = 50 pF, α = 0.1, 1.8 V, I<sub>leak</sub> = 10 µA):
answer.pre:
P<sub>sw</sub> at 100 MHz = 0.1 × 50 pF × 3.24 × 10⁸ = 1.62 mW
P<sub>leak</sub> = 1.8 × 10 µA = 18 µW
crossover f = I<sub>leak</sub>/(αCV<sub>DD</sub>) = 10 µA/(0.1 × 50 pF × 1.8 V) = 1.11 MHz

answer: Above about 1.1 MHz switching dominates (90 to 1 at 100 MHz); below it, and when the clock stops, leakage dominates. Lowering V<sub>t</sub> by 100 mV with S = 100 mV/decade multiplies leakage by 10 and moves the crossover to 11.1 MHz.

Short-circuit share for one gate: a 20 fF node at α = 0.1, 1.8 V and 100 MHz switches 0.1 × 20 fF × 3.24 V² × 10⁸ Hz = 0.648 µW, so the 42.7 nW of short-circuit power above is about 7% of it. With slow input edges this share grows in proportion to t<sub>r</sub>, which is why timing tools limit slew.

How each term is cut: switching power by a lower V<sub>DD</sub> (square law), lower α (clock gating, less glitching) and smaller C (minimum sizes off the critical path); short-circuit power by sharp, balanced edges; leakage by high-V<sub>t</sub> cells, stacks and power gating of idle blocks.

bank.q: Describe the precharge and evaluate phases of a dynamic CMOS gate. Explain charge sharing, the keeper, clock feedthrough and why domino logic is needed to cascade gates. Draw a CVSL gate and explain its operation. A 40 fF dynamic node at 1.8 V shares charge with an 8 fF internal node at 0 V: find the final voltage.
outline: two phases and the monotonic-input rule
charge sharing formula with numbers, keeper
answer: Circuit: precharge pMOS from V<sub>DD</sub> to node X, nMOS pull-down network from X to a clocked foot nMOS, foot to ground; both clock transistors take φ. An N-input gate needs N + 2 transistors.

Precharge (φ = 0): pMOS on, foot off, X → V<sub>DD</sub>. Evaluate (φ = 1): pMOS off, foot on; X discharges if the PDN conducts, otherwise floats high on its capacitance. Once discharged, X cannot recover until the next precharge, so inputs must be stable or only rise during evaluation.

answer.text: Charge sharing: an internal stack node at 0 V connects to X when an upper transistor turns on but the path to ground stays open:

answer: A 0.3 V drop can reach the switching point of the output inverter. Cures: precharge internal nodes, keep C<sub>int</sub> small, add a keeper (weak pMOS from V<sub>DD</sub> to X with its gate driven by the output inverter, on while X is high). The keeper must lose to the PDN, so it is sized weak.
Leakage: with no keeper the node droops; 10 nA on 50 fF loses 0.3 V in 1.5 µs, which sets a lowest clock frequency.

Clock feedthrough: the clock edge couples through the gate-drain capacitance of the precharge transistor and briefly pushes X above V<sub>DD</sub> (or below during evaluation), a noise source on the dynamic node.

Domino: X is high during precharge; fed straight into the next dynamic gate it would turn its nMOS on and discharge it wrongly. A static inverter after X gives an output that is 0 during precharge and can only rise during evaluation, so stages fall in sequence. Domino gates are non-inverting (AND, OR).

CVSL: two complementary nMOS networks (F and F̄) pull down the two outputs Q̄ and Q; two pMOS loads are cross-coupled (each gate on the other output). When one network conducts, its output falls, turning on the opposite pMOS, which pulls the other output to V<sub>DD</sub> and switches its own load off. Full swing, no static current, both polarities, but the nMOS must overpower the still-on pMOS while switching, so it is ratioed during transitions.
Check: 1.50 V is the 40 fF node's charge (72 fC) spread over 48 fF; with C<sub>int</sub> ≤ C<sub>X</sub>/5 = 8 fF the drop stays at or below 0.3 V.

bank.q: A CMOS inverter at V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.2 V has k<sub>n</sub> = 300 µA/V², k<sub>p</sub> = 150 µA/V², V<sub>tn</sub> = |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.35 V and drives C<sub>L</sub> = 20 fF. Find t<sub>PHL</sub>, t<sub>PLH</sub> and t<sub>p</sub> by the average-current method, check t<sub>PHL</sub> with the RC model, find the k<sub>p</sub> for equal edges, and the frequency of a 51-stage ring oscillator of these inverters.

answer.text: Saturation currents (overdrive 1.2 − 0.35 = 0.85 V):

answer: Charge to the 50% point: C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>/2 = 20 fF × 0.6 V = 12 fC.

answer.text: Delays:

answer: RC check: R<sub>eq,n</sub> ≈ 0.75 × 1.2 V / 108.4 µA = 8.30 kΩ, so t<sub>PHL</sub> ≈ 0.69 × 8.30 kΩ × 20 fF = 0.115 ns, within 4% of 0.111 ns.

Equal edges need I<sub>p</sub> = I<sub>n</sub>, so k<sub>p</sub> = k<sub>n</sub> = 300 µA/V²: double the pMOS width. Then t<sub>PLH</sub> = t<sub>PHL</sub> = 0.111 ns, but the input capacitance rises and the drain capacitance adds to C<sub>L</sub> a little.

Load dependence: all three delays are proportional to C<sub>L</sub>. At 40 fF, for example a fan-out twice as large, t<sub>PHL</sub> = 0.222 ns, t<sub>PLH</sub> = 0.443 ns and t<sub>p</sub> = 0.332 ns.

Ring oscillator: f = 1/(2Nt<sub>p</sub>) = 1/(2 × 51 × 0.166 ns) = 1/(16.9 ns) ≈ 59 MHz. In the ring each inverter drives the next inverter, so C<sub>L</sub> must be the real stage load for this to hold.
Rise and fall times by the RC model: t<sub>f</sub> ≈ 2.2 × 8.30 kΩ × 20 fF = 0.37 ns, and t<sub>r</sub> twice that with the half-strength pMOS.
Check of units: fC ÷ µA = ns; 12/108.4 = 0.111. The ratio t<sub>PLH</sub>/t<sub>PHL</sub> = 2 equals k<sub>n</sub>/k<sub>p</sub>, as it must when the overdrives are equal.

Regions during the fall: the nMOS stays saturated while V<sub>out</sub> > V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.85 V and is linear from 0.85 V down to the 0.6 V point, where its current is slightly lower, so the true t<sub>PHL</sub> is a few per cent above 0.111 ns.

Effect of the supply: at 1.5 V the overdrive is 1.15 V, I<sub>n</sub> = 150 × 1.3225 = 198.4 µA and the charge is 20 fF × 0.75 V = 15 fC, so t<sub>PHL</sub> = 15 fC / 198.4 µA = 0.076 ns. A 25% higher supply makes the gate 32% faster, at (1.5/1.2)² = 1.56 times the switching energy.

bank.q: A path is NAND2 → NOR2 → inverter. The path input capacitance is 8 units and the load is 288 units, with no branching. Using g(NAND2) = 4/3, g(NOR2) = 5/3, p(NAND2) = p(NOR2) = 2 and p(INV) = 1, find G, H, F, the best stage effort, the least delay and the input capacitance and transistor widths of each gate. Is three the right number of stages?
outline: log<sub>4</sub> F for the stage count

answer.text: Work back from the load, C<sub>in</sub> = g × C<sub>out</sub>/f̂:
answer.pre:
inverter: C<sub>in</sub> = 1   × 288   / 4.309 = 66.84 units
NOR2:     C<sub>in</sub> = 5/3 × 66.84 / 4.309 = 25.85 units
NAND2:    C<sub>in</sub> = 4/3 × 25.85 / 4.309 =  8.00 units  (matches the given input)

answer.text: Widths (unit inverter nMOS 1, pMOS 2, input 3 units; unit NOR2 nMOS 1, pMOS 4, input 5; unit NAND2 nMOS 2, pMOS 2, input 4):

answer: Stage check: each stage has f = gh = 4.31 (NAND2: 4/3 × 25.85/8 = 4.31; NOR2: 5/3 × 66.84/25.85 = 4.31; inverter: 288/66.84 = 4.31), so delays are 6.31, 6.31 and 5.31τ, total 17.93τ.

Stage count: log<sub>4</sub> 80 = 3.16, so three stages is right. Two stages are impossible here without changing the logic, and adding a pair of inverters (N = 5) gives 5 × 80<sup>1/5</sup> + 7 = 5 × 2.40 + 7 = 19.0τ, slower.
Conclusion: D ≈ 17.9τ with the gates growing about 4.3 times per stage; the NOR2's wide series pMOS (20.7 units) is the costly part, which is why designers prefer NAND-based paths.

Terms used: g is the logical effort (input capacitance of the gate relative to an inverter of equal drive), h = C<sub>out</sub>/C<sub>in</sub> the electrical effort, p the parasitic delay, and τ the delay of an ideal inverter with no parasitics driving an identical one. NOR2 has g = 5/3 because its two series pMOS must each be 4 wide to match the unit inverter, giving 1 + 4 = 5 units per input against 3.

In time units: with τ = 15 ps, D = 17.93 × 15 = 269 ps. If the NAND2 output also had to drive a second, identical NOR2, the branching effort would be B = 2, F = 160, f̂ = 160<sup>1/3</sup> = 5.43 and D = 3 × 5.43 + 5 = 21.3τ, so branching costs 3.4τ even with the best sizes.

bank.q: A driver of 2 kΩ with 15 fF of drain capacitance drives a wire of 400 Ω and 50 fF (lumped at its end) to a branch point. From there 300 Ω leads to gate G1 (30 fF) and 600 Ω to gate G2 (60 fF). Find the Elmore delays and 50% delays at G1 and G2. What happens at G2 if the driver is made twice as wide (1 kΩ)? Then find the Elmore delay of a NAND3 pull-down with 2 kΩ per transistor, internal nodes of 5 fF and an output of 30 fF.
outline: stack: n² growth and input order
answer: Tree: driver 2 kΩ to node d (15 fF); 400 Ω to node b (50 fF); 300 Ω from b to G1 (30 fF); 600 Ω from b to G2 (60 fF).

answer.text: Shared resistance from the driver (kΩ):
Sums (fF × kΩ = ps):

answer: Stronger driver (1 kΩ; ignore its larger drain capacitance): τ<sub>G2</sub> = 15×1.0 + 50×1.4 + 30×1.4 + 60×2.0 = 15 + 70 + 42 + 120 = 247 ps, 39% less. The 155 ps saved is 1 kΩ × 155 fF, the whole capacitance of the tree times the resistance removed.

answer.text: NAND3 pull-down (nodes x<sub>1</sub>, x<sub>2</sub> from the bottom):

answer: The internal nodes cost 30 ps. If the latest input drives the top transistor, the lower nodes are already discharged when it arrives and the delay falls towards 0.69 × 180 = 124 ps. Each extra series transistor adds both resistance and a node, so stack delay grows roughly as n².
Check: τ<sub>G2</sub> > τ<sub>G1</sub> because G2 has the larger capacitance behind the larger resistance; the side branch adds only 72 ps to G2 against 81 ps for its own path to G1.

Rule used: the Elmore delay at node i is τ<sub>i</sub> = Σ<sub>k</sub> C<sub>k</sub>R<sub>ik</sub>, where R<sub>ik</sub> is the resistance shared by the path from the source to i and the path from the source to k. It is the first moment of the impulse response, an upper bound on the 50% delay of an RC tree, and 0.69τ is used as the 50% estimate.

Driver width and its own capacitance: a driver twice as wide also has about twice the drain capacitance. With 30 fF at node d the delay to G2 becomes 247 + 1.0 kΩ × 15 fF = 262 ps, still 35% better than 402 ps, so widening still pays here because the driver resistance was the largest term.

bank.q: Design a pseudo-nMOS NOR gate for V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V, V<sub>tn</sub> = |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.45 V, with each nMOS k<sub>n</sub> = 120 µA/V², so that V<sub>OL</sub> ≤ 0.2 V. Find the largest k<sub>p</sub>, the static current and power, and compare with a static CMOS NOR of the same fan-in.
outline: transistor count and input capacitance compared
answer: Circuit: N nMOS in parallel from output to ground, one pMOS from V<sub>DD</sub> to the output with its gate at 0 V.
Worst case for V<sub>OL</sub>: only one input high, so one nMOS (k<sub>n</sub> = 120 µA/V²) fights the load. More inputs high only lower V<sub>OL</sub>.

answer.text: Driver current at V<sub>OL</sub> = 0.2 V (linear, overdrive 1.35 V):

answer: Load: saturated because V<sub>OL</sub> = 0.2 V ≤ |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.45 V. (k<sub>p</sub>/2)(1.8 − 0.45)² = 0.911k<sub>p</sub> must not exceed 30 µA, so k<sub>p</sub> ≤ 32.9 µA/V², a ratio k<sub>n</sub>/k<sub>p</sub> ≥ 3.65. A designer leaves margin: with k<sub>p</sub> = 30 µA/V² the load current is 27.3 µA and V<sub>OL</sub> = (2.7 − √(7.29 − 1.82))/2 = 0.181 V.
Static current with the output low: 30 µA; power 1.8 V × 30 µA = 54 µW per gate while low, zero (only leakage) while high.
Rising edge: the 30 µA pull-up charges, say, 30 fF to 0.9 V in about 30 fF × 0.9 V / 30 µA = 0.9 ns, much slower than the fall, which is set by 120 µA/V² devices.

answer.text: Comparison for a 4-input NOR:

head: Pseudo-nMOS
Static CMOS
rows: nMOS + a pMOS four times wider (series stack)

answer: Conclusion: pseudo-nMOS suits wide NOR gates (decoders, PLA planes) where area and input load matter and the gate is low only briefly; static CMOS is preferred everywhere else.

Two inputs high: the two nMOS in parallel act as k = 240 µA/V², so 240[1.35V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2] = 30 µA gives V<sub>OL</sub>² − 2.7V<sub>OL</sub> + 0.25 = 0 and V<sub>OL</sub> = (2.7 − √6.29)/2 = 0.096 V, lower as expected.

Falling edge: one nMOS gives (120/2)(1.35)² = 109.4 µA while saturated, but the load still takes 30 µA, so about 79.4 µA discharges the node. For 30 fF to 0.9 V: 27 fC / 79.4 µA = 0.34 ns. The fall is slowed by the always-on load, and the rise is slower still.

bank.q: A CMOS chip has 10<sup>6</sup> switching nodes of 20 fF each, V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.2 V, α = 0.2 and f = 500 MHz; its leakage current is 50 mA. Find the dynamic, leakage and total power and the energy per cycle. DVFS then moves it to 0.9 V and 300 MHz, where leakage falls to 35 mA. Find the new figures and the savings.
answer: Total switched capacitance: 10<sup>6</sup> × 20 fF = 20 nF.

answer.text: At 1.2 V, 500 MHz:
answer.pre:
P<sub>dyn</sub> = 0.2 × 20 nF × 1.44 V² × 500 MHz = 2.88 W
P<sub>leak</sub> = 1.2 V × 50 mA = 0.060 W
P<sub>total</sub> = 2.94 W
dynamic energy per cycle = 2.88 W / 500 MHz = 5.76 nJ

answer.text: At 0.9 V, 300 MHz:
answer.pre:
ratio = (0.9/1.2)² × (300/500) = 0.5625 × 0.6 = 0.3375
P<sub>dyn</sub> = 2.88 × 0.3375 = 0.972 W
P<sub>leak</sub> = 0.9 V × 35 mA = 0.0315 W
P<sub>total</sub> = 1.004 W
dynamic energy per cycle = 0.972 W / 300 MHz = 3.24 nJ

answer: Savings: total power falls by 66% (2.94 → 1.00 W). Energy per cycle falls by 44% (5.76 → 3.24 nJ), exactly (0.9/1.2)² = 0.5625, because energy depends only on V².

Why the frequency must drop: gate delay rises as V<sub>DD</sub> falls (less overdrive), so 0.9 V can only support a slower clock; the table entry 0.9 V / 300 MHz must be checked at the slow corner. The period grows from 2 ns to 3.33 ns, so the critical path may slow by up to 67% at 0.9 V and still meet timing.
Order of change: going down, lower f first then V; going up, raise V first then f.
Leakage share: 2% of the power at 500 MHz, 3% at 300 MHz. If the chip then idles with the clock gated, only the 31.5 mW of leakage remains, and power gating idle blocks is the next step.

answer.text: Energy for a fixed task of 3 × 10⁹ cycles:
answer.pre:
at 500 MHz: time 6 s,  energy 2.94 W × 6 s  = 17.6 J (leakage 0.36 J)
at 300 MHz: time 10 s, energy 1.004 W × 10 s = 10.0 J (leakage 0.32 J)
saving 1 − 10.0/17.6 = 43%

answer: The task takes longer at the lower point, so leakage acts for longer: here its energy barely falls (0.36 → 0.32 J). When leakage is a large share of power, running slowly can cost energy, and the better choice is to run fast and then power down (race to idle).

bank.q: An nMOS pass transistor at V<sub>DD</sub> = 2.5 V has V<sub>t0</sub> = 0.45 V, γ = 0.5 V<sup>1/2</sup> and 2φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.6 V. Find the highest level it passes with gate and input at 2.5 V, and the level after a second nMOS switch whose gate is driven by that weak level. How does a transmission gate fix this? Give the transistor count of a TG 2:1 multiplexer.
outline: source is the output for a passed 1
second switch with a weak gate
TG: pMOS passes the top, nMOS the bottom
answer: For a passed 1 the output Y is the lower terminal, so it is the source: V<sub>GS</sub> = 2.5 − V<sub>Y</sub>, and the device cuts off when V<sub>Y</sub> = 2.5 − V<sub>tn</sub>(V<sub>Y</sub>), with V<sub>SB</sub> = V<sub>Y</sub>.
Result: V<sub>Y</sub> ≈ 1.68 V with V<sub>tn</sub> ≈ 0.82 V; without body effect it would be 2.05 V.

Second switch: its gate is at 1.68 V and its input at 2.5 V. It now stops at 1.68 − V<sub>tn</sub>(V<sub>Y2</sub>); iterating the same way gives V<sub>Y2</sub> ≈ 0.99 V. Drops add when a passed level drives a gate, so pass networks must never chain gate-to-gate like this.
Effect downstream: 1.68 V into a 2.5 V inverter leaves the pMOS with V<sub>SG</sub> = 0.82 V > 0.45 V, so it stays on and static current flows; 0.99 V may not even be read as a 1.

Transmission gate: a pMOS (gate C̄ = 0 V) in parallel with the nMOS (gate C). As Y rises, the nMOS weakens but the pMOS, whose source is at the 2.5 V input, stays fully on, so Y reaches 2.5 V; for a passed 0 the nMOS does the work. Its resistance stays nearly constant over the swing.

TG 2:1 mux: two TGs (4 transistors) plus an inverter for S̄ (2) = 6 transistors, against 12 for a static AOI22 version with its inverters. One TG is always on, so the output is always driven; a restoring inverter is added after a few switches because TGs have no gain.
Check: 2.5 − 0.818 = 1.682 V, consistent; the second level 0.99 V is about 0.69 V below its 1.68 V gate, a larger threshold because the source is higher.

Passing a 0: the nMOS source is then the 0 V side, V<sub>GS</sub> stays 2.5 V and V<sub>SB</sub> = 0, so it pulls Y fully to 0 V. A pMOS alone is the mirror image: it passes a strong 1 but stops a 0 at about |V<sub>tp</sub>| plus its body effect.

Level restorer: a weak pMOS from V<sub>DD</sub> to the inverter input, with its gate driven by the inverter output. When Y reaches 1.68 V the inverter output falls, turns this pMOS on, and it pulls Y to 2.5 V, ending the static current. It must be weak enough that the pass transistor can still pull Y low against it.

bank.q: A 4 mm wire with r = 0.25 Ω/µm and c = 0.2 fF/µm connects a driver of 1 kΩ to a 20 fF load. Estimate its delay with the lumped RC, distributed RC and Elmore models. Evaluate inserting 1, 2 or 3 repeaters (each like the driver, 1 kΩ and 20 fF), and then repeaters four times stronger (250 Ω, 80 fF). Neglect repeater intrinsic delay. What should a designer conclude?

answer.text: One segment (driver R<sub>d</sub>, wire, load C<sub>L</sub>):
answer.pre:
distributed: 0.69R<sub>d</sub>(C<sub>w</sub> + C<sub>L</sub>) + 0.38R<sub>w</sub>C<sub>w</sub> + 0.69R<sub>w</sub>C<sub>L</sub>
           = 0.69×1k×820f + 0.38×1k×800f + 0.69×1k×20f
           = 565.8 + 304.0 + 13.8 = 883.6 ps
lumped RC:   0.69(R<sub>d</sub> + R<sub>w</sub>)(C<sub>w</sub> + C<sub>L</sub>) = 0.69 × 2k × 820f = 1131.6 ps
Elmore:      R<sub>d</sub>(C<sub>w</sub> + C<sub>L</sub>) + R<sub>w</sub>(C<sub>w</sub>/2 + C<sub>L</sub>) = 820 + 420 = 1240 ps → ×0.69 = 855.6 ps

answer: The lumped model is 28% pessimistic; Elmore × 0.69 is within 3% of the distributed estimate here because the driver term dominates.

answer.text: Repeaters: n segments of 4/n mm; each segment drives the next repeater (or the final load):
Working for two weak segments (2 mm each: 500 Ω, 400 fF):
Working for two strong segments:

answer: Analysis: with the weak 1 kΩ driver, 566 of the 884 ps is the driver charging the whole wire, so cutting the wire helps little (884 → 697 ps with three repeaters). The wire's own distributed term (304 ps) is what repeaters remove: two segments have 2 × 76 = 152 ps of it, three have 3 × 33.8 = 101 ps, following L².

With four-times-stronger drivers the driver term shrinks fourfold, so the wire term becomes a larger share, and repeaters pay off more: 459 → 342 ps for one repeater. Beyond two or three, the gain flattens and real repeaters add their own intrinsic delay (neglected here), so there is an optimum count and size.

Conclusion: first size the driver so its resistance is comparable with the wire's, then insert repeaters so each segment's wire delay is about equal to a repeater delay. For this wire, strong drivers with one or two repeaters cut the delay from 884 ps to about 340 ps, 2.6 times faster. Checks: every segment formula adds driver, wire and load terms; the four-segment numbers approach a limit as expected.

bank.q: Implement F = A·(B + C) in static CMOS, pseudo-nMOS and domino logic, and Y = A ? B : C (a 2:1 multiplexer) with transmission gates. Compare transistor count, output levels, static current, clocking, input capacitance and robustness, and recommend a style for a standard-cell datapath and for a wide decoder.
outline: static CMOS compound gate plus inverter
answer: Static CMOS: NOT(A·(B + C)) is one compound gate: PDN A in series with (B ∥ C), PUN A ∥ (B series C); widths nMOS 2, 2, 2 and pMOS A 2, B and C 4 for unit drive. g<sub>A</sub> = 4/3, g<sub>B</sub> = g<sub>C</sub> = 2. Add an inverter for F: 6 + 2 = 8 transistors, two stages, full swing, no static current.

Pseudo-nMOS: the same PDN (3 nMOS) with one pMOS load, plus an inverter: 4 + 2 = 6 transistors. V<sub>OL</sub> > 0 (for example 0.21 V with k<sub>n</sub>/k<sub>p</sub> = 5 at 2.5 V), static current whenever the PDN conducts (40 µA, 100 µW in that example), slow rising edge.

Domino: precharge pMOS, PDN (A in series with B ∥ C), foot nMOS, output inverter: 1 + 3 + 1 + 2 = 7 transistors, 8 with a keeper. Output F is non-inverting, as needed. Inputs drive only nMOS (low input capacitance, fast), but it needs a clock, inputs that only rise during evaluation, a keeper against leakage, and care with charge sharing: the node between A and B ∥ C must be kept small or precharged (a 10 fF node on 50 fF drops X to 1.5 V at 1.8 V).

TG multiplexer: TG1 passes B when A = 1 (nMOS gate A, pMOS gate Ā), TG2 passes C when A = 0. Four transistors plus an inverter for Ā = 6. Full swing both ways, no static current, but no gain: a restoring inverter is needed after a few stages and the select must have both polarities.

answer.text: Comparison:

answer: Delay view: by logical effort the static gate's B and C inputs have g = 2, the domino inputs about 2/3 of a unit nMOS-only gate, so domino is about 1.5 to 2 times faster per stage, which is why it was used on critical paths of fast processors.
Power view: domino precharges every cycle, so its node has α up to 1 and its clock load adds power; pseudo-nMOS burns static power; static CMOS switches only when the logic changes.

Recommendation, standard-cell datapath: static CMOS (compound gates, TG multiplexers and XORs inside cells) because it is robust across corners, needs no clock and has no static current; synthesis and timing tools handle it directly.

Recommendation, wide decoder (for example 6-input NOR rows of a ROM or PLA): pseudo-nMOS or a precharged dynamic NOR, because a static 6-input NOR needs six series pMOS with huge input capacitance; accept static current or clocking for the area and speed.
Check of counts: static 6 + 2 = 8; pseudo 3 + 1 + 2 = 6; domino 3 + 2 + 2 (+1 keeper) = 7 (8); TG 4 + 2 = 6.

bank.q: A datapath block runs at 1.0 V and 1 GHz with α = 0.15 and 80 pF of switched capacitance; it leaks 3 mW. It is busy 40% of the time; while idle with the clock running, its clock tree still burns 4 mW. Evaluate (a) no power management, (b) clock gating, (c) clock gating plus power gating with long idle periods, and (d) running continuously at 0.8 V and 400 MHz (enough for the same work), where leakage is 2.2 mW. Recommend a design, including cell and sizing choices.
outline: DVFS: same work at lower V and f
answer: Busy dynamic power: P = αCV<sup>2</sup>f = 0.15 × 80 pF × 1.0² × 1 GHz = 12 mW.

answer.text: Average power for each option:

answer: Explanation of (b): clock gating removes the 4 mW clock-tree power during the 60% idle time, saving 2.4 mW (24%), at the cost of an integrated clock-gating cell per register group.

Explanation of (c): power gating removes leakage during idle time, saving another 1.8 mW. It pays only if each idle period exceeds the break-even time; with, say, 1.5 nJ per sleep-wake cycle and 3 mW leakage that is 0.5 µs, so short idle bursts should use only clock gating. It needs a header switch, retention flip-flops and isolation cells.

Explanation of (d): the same work done 40% of the time at 1 GHz can be spread over all the time at 400 MHz. Lower frequency allows 0.8 V, and dynamic power scales as V²f: 12 × 0.64 × 0.4 = 3.07 mW. Energy per operation falls by 36% (0.8²), so (d) wins at 5.27 mW, 48% below (a).

Combining: at 0.8 V and 400 MHz the block is never idle, so gating adds little; if the workload varies, DVFS for the busy phases plus clock gating (and power gating for long idles) gives the lowest average.

Cell choices: use high-V<sub>t</sub> cells on non-critical paths; if, say, 70% of the leakage comes from such cells and high-V<sub>t</sub> cuts their leakage by 5 times, the 2.2 mW becomes 2.2 × (0.3 + 0.7/5) = 0.97 mW. But lowering V<sub>DD</sub> to 0.8 V slows gates, so the critical path must still close at 400 MHz: keep low-V<sub>t</sub> cells and logical-effort sizing (stage effort about 4) on it.
Sizing: oversized gates off the critical path add switched capacitance; downsizing them lowers C and so P<sub>dyn</sub> directly, at no cost in clock speed.

Recommendation: option (d) with clock gating for any idle time, high-V<sub>t</sub> cells off the critical path and minimum sizes where timing allows. Expected power about 3.07 + 0.97 ≈ 4.0 mW, 60% below the unmanaged 10.2 mW. Check: 0.15 × 80 × 10⁻¹² × 1 × 10⁹ = 0.012 W; 12 × 0.256 = 3.07.

answer.text: Energy per operation (0.4 × 10⁹ operations each second in every option):

answer: Risks to weigh: (c) needs retention and isolation and a wake-up latency the system must tolerate; (d) needs a regulator able to supply 0.8 V and timing closed at 0.8 V at the slow corner. If the workload later needs 1 GHz bursts, a DVFS table with both points is the robust design.
